Review:
The problem is relevant to the current mechanical-memory/hysteretic-metamaterials context and is unusually well anchored in the supplied rows. The decomposition into an additive window translation and a width change is a sensible effective-parameter question, and the identifiability question is the strongest part: 16 ordered events with no timestamps or reversal rows cannot identify network_C’s graph, so reporting an equivalence class and a minimal discriminating measurement is a genuine contribution. The empirical summaries check out. My linear check gives S046 ≈0.459 N/cm and S007 ≈0.070 N/cm, with residuals ≤0.06 N and ≤0.004 N, so the linear-spring null result is credible; the paired loading/unloading gap for S046 is ≈0.03 N. All 15 successive transitions change exactly one rotor, and events 9–16 repeat 1–8 exactly. In pair_A the half-width shrinks 7.2→4.6 cm while the neighbour-induced centre shift grows ≈0.1, 0.6, 1.2 cm (rotor 1) and ≈0.4, 1.9, 4.4 cm (rotor 2); pair_B shows large centre shifts (11.1, 5.5 cm) with nearly invariant half-widths (4.1 vs 4.0; 11.4 vs 11.7 cm). These are relevant, testable regularities.

But the relevance is not yet field-level. The additive-bias/multiplicative-gain decomposition is essentially a moving-Preisach/mean-field interaction ansatz, long established in hysteresis modeling; the mechanical lever-arm realization and the graph-identifiability angle are the new parts, and the problem should say so explicitly rather than presenting the decomposition as novel. The evidence is one iteratively adjusted four-rotor device, with no replicates and ±0.1 cm thresholds; generalization to “multi-rotor hysteretic devices” is asserted, not demonstrated. The width-invariance test in pair_B is low-power: 0.1–0.3 cm differences are at or near threshold uncertainty. P2 as stated (“collapse across rotors with k_c = 0.07 N/cm”) is already in tension with the data: the ℓ² prefactors are ≈0.05 cm/cm² for rotor 1 and ≈0.19 cm/cm² for rotor 2, so a rotor-specific moment-arm factor is required. P3’s “only its flip position” ignores coupling back-action on neighbours. P4’s attractor reading is a hypothesis, not a measured stability result.

Feedback:
1) Define the effective torque model explicitly (e.g., T_i = T_i⁰(θ_i) + b_i(s_j,ℓ) + k_i(s_j,ℓ)θ_i) and state that bias/gain are model-relative, not unique physical components. 2) Position the work against moving-Preisach/mean-field hysteresis and mechanical-memory studies; specify the incremental prediction that differs. 3) Make P2 rotor-specific: fit b(ℓ) = b₀ + c_iℓ² and test whether c_i is predicted by the measured moment arms and stop angles; the current data suggest c₂/c₁ ≈ 3.7. 4) Restate P3 conditionally: preload changes only the target flip if it does not alter coupling-spring extensions; otherwise predict neighbour shifts. 5) For identifiability, give a concrete minimal design: clamp all but one rotor, sweep each of the 2³ neighbour states, record reversal positions and repeats, and report the equivalence class plus the measurement that breaks it. 6) Add repeat thresholds and propagate ±0.1 cm; a 0.1–0.3 cm width change is not decisive without replicates. 7) Keep reversal positions and times unknown; do not infer them from event extrema. These changes would raise relevance from a careful single-device model-discrimination study to a transferable method.

Rating (1-5): 4
